---
title: "Your first compression"
subtitle: "Encode, write, and read a spike train"
---

## Install

```bash
pip install spikepack[zarr]   # drop [zarr] if you only need the Blosc container
```

## Encode a spike train

`encode_times` takes a sorted array of event times in seconds and returns
delta-encoded integer ticks plus the metadata needed to invert the transform:

```python
import numpy as np
from spikepack import encode_times, decode_times

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
times = np.cumsum(rng.exponential(scale=1 / 50, size=100_000))  # ~50 Hz Poisson train

deltas, meta = encode_times(times, quantization_us=100)
print(deltas.dtype, meta)

recovered = decode_times(deltas, meta)
print(np.max(np.abs(recovered - times)))  # <= 50e-6 (half a tick)
```

## Write and read a container

`write_blosc`/`read_blosc` wrap `encode_times` with array compression and an
on-disk layout, and optionally carry a per-event integer label (e.g. a unit or
cluster id):

```python
from spikepack import write_blosc, read_blosc

labels = rng.integers(0, 50, size=times.size)  # e.g. cluster id per spike

write_blosc("my_recording", times_seconds=times, labels=labels, quantization_us=100)
out = read_blosc("my_recording")

out["times"]   # float64 seconds, reconstructed
out["labels"]  # original labels, exact
out["meta"]    # quantization_us, dtype, n_events, ...
```

`write_zarr`/`read_zarr` have the same signature and store the same information
in a standard Zarr group instead — see the [Blosc vs Zarr how-to](../how-to/blosc-vs-zarr.qmd)
for when to prefer one over the other.
